title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: one woman is Mom, Auntie, Doctor and Grandma, depending on who's calling. A Rig Veda verse says the one truth is called by many names

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: shruti, what is heard, carried mouth to ear, and a poet who fashioned his hymn like a chariot. Did you teach someone a line by voice alone? Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

At a family party, one woman answers to everything. Her kids call her Mom. Her nephew calls her Auntie. At the hospital that morning, her patients called her Doctor. Her granddaughter, toddling across the room, calls her something that sounds like Nani. Four names, and she turns her head for every one. Nobody at the party is confused. Each name catches a different side of her, the side that person knows. She's one person, called many ways. Deep inside the Rig Veda, in a long and puzzling hymn, there's a verse that says something very like this about the divine. Today, that verse, and a look back over the week.
screen: `MOM, AUNTIE, DOCTOR, NANI.` → `ONE PERSON, MANY NAMES.` → `A VERSE DEEP IN THE RIG VEDA.`

segments.voice: The Rig Veda's hymns praise many gods. Agni, the fire. Indra, who wields the thunderbolt and frees the waters. Varuna, keeper of cosmic order. Mitra, the friend. Soma, the sacred drink. Ushas, the dawn. A hymn may praise its god in the highest terms, and another hymn may do the same for a different god. Then, in a long riddle-hymn full of puzzles, comes this verse. In paraphrase: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, and the heavenly bird with lovely wings. What is one, the wise speak of in many ways. They call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan. Ekam sat. One being, one truth. Many names. Readers have heard this verse in more than one way. Some hear it as saying that all the gods are faces of one divine reality. Vedanta teachers later read it as pointing to Brahman. Others hear a poet's riddle about the sun, or about speech itself. The verse doesn't settle it. And that fits the week we've walked. We finished Gaudapada's Karika, with space in the pots and a torch held still, pointing to one self that only seems many. Then we opened the Rig Veda: a fire hymn that asks Agni to come close, and seers who heard hymns and carried them by voice. Many forms, many voices, and running through them, a hint of one.
screen: `MANY GODS, EACH PRAISED IN TURN.` · `ONE BEING, CALLED IN MANY WAYS.` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · `THIS WEEK: ONE SEEMING MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the names you go by. Sit, and let the breath settle. Silently, list the names people call you. Your given name. A nickname. A family title: son, sister, Dad, Auntie. A work name. Notice how each one brings a slightly different you to mind. Then let the names go quiet, one by one, and rest in the one who answers to all of them. If you pray, you can call the divine by the name you love best, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns to many gods, and inside them a verse that says the wise call the one truth by many names. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Today, notice when someone calls you by a name nobody else uses, and what side of you it reaches. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Hindus who quote 'ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti', from Rig Veda 1.164.46, use it to say that the one truth is called by many names, and that many forms of the divine are one.

fork.setup: you're the poet. you've praised Indra, Varuna and Agni in turn. someone asks: so which one is really it? what do you answer?
options: the wise call the one in many ways.
fork.reveal: the verse names Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni and more, and says: what is one, the wise speak of in many ways.

original.note: Sanskrit: one being, one truth. From Rig Veda 1.164.46: ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Rig Veda is a crowd of separate gods.
what it means: it praises many gods, and one verse says the wise call the one by many names.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.164.46, inside the long riddle hymn of Dirghatamas, read by some as about all gods, by Vedanta as Brahman, by others as about the sun or speech.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.164.46 (they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, and the heavenly well-winged Garutman; what is one, the sages call in many ways; they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan)

notes: Rig Veda 1.164.46 paraphrased (no PD translation on the validator list). Confirm the gloss of Garutman as 'the heavenly bird with lovely wings'.
The god descriptions (Indra freeing the waters, Varuna keeper of order, Mitra the friend) are standard summaries, not quotations. Confirm.
'Each hymn tends to praise its god as if that god were the greatest' describes what scholars call henotheism; the term is left out. Confirm the wording is fair.
Trapdoor names Dirghatamas as the seer of 1.164 (from the tradition's index); confirm.
Week-end recap covers days 1240–1245 briefly (the Karika's last days, then the Rig Veda's opening).
Editor: softened the sweeping 'each hymn' claim about praise of the gods to 'a hymn may'.
